speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: asked the Prime Minister in view of the bankruptcy of cryptocurrency trading platform FTX (a) how will this affect Singapore's financial market and economy; and (b) how many retail traders in Singapore are affected.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) what further steps will be taken to strengthen the system for cryptocurrency companies with non-licensed offshore exchanges that have operations in Singapore; and (b) whether the bar will be raised to prevent local retail investors without adequate risk knowledge or direct funding means from participating in investments.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: asked the Prime Minister in light of the recent bankruptcy of cryptocurrency exchange FTX (a) what are the lessons drawn from this incident; and (b) what are the immediate and long-term steps that will be taken by MAS to help mitigate against consumer risks in cryptocurrency trading.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Prime Minister (a) whether MAS will consider leading a specific study into the regulatory lessons to be learnt from the collapse of cryptocurrency exchanges, such as Terra and FTX; and (b) whether there needs to be tighter requirements to ensure the stability of regulated cryptocurrency exchanges in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Prime Minister whether the Government intends to introduce further measures or safeguards to regulate cryptocurrency trading or investment, as well as to protect Singaporean retail investors in general.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: asked the Prime Minister whether the recommendations in MAS’ ongoing public consultation can be expedited, to reduce the risk of consumer harm from cryptocurrency trading and to support the development of stablecoins as a credible medium of exchange in the digital asset ecosystem.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Prime Minister in view of the various insolvencies of cryptocurrency exchanges and extreme volatility in the cryptocurrency markets in the last year (a) how will this affect our efforts to become a robust global blockchain and fintech hub; (b) whether MAS will consider further regulatory measures to prevent any contagion into the wider cryptocurrency, fintech and financial markets; and (c) if so, what are they.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) what is the impact of the recent bankruptcy of cryptocurrency exchange FTX on Temasek Holdings’ investment in FTX; and (b) what are the due diligence or measures undertaken prior to investments in cryptocurrency trading platforms, such as FTX.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance given that the Government does not direct GIC and Temasek Holdings’ individual investment decisions but holds their boards accountable for their performance, whether the Government will consider creating a bipartisan Standing Select Committee of Parliament that meets regularly to question the boards of the two sovereign wealth funds on their performance, strategies and risk management approaches, on a confidential basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance in light of MAS’ proposed measures to reduce cryptocurrency trading risks, whether similar suggestions have been promulgated to Government-related investment entities, such as GIC and Temasek Holdings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether there are regulations or a governance framework as to the basic level of due diligence to be observed by entities listed in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution handling Government assets which involve the investment of significant public funds; and (b) whether there are ongoing due diligence or audit requirements for these investments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether the Ministry tracks the extent of concentration of investments by GIC and Temasek Holdings investment vehicles either by (i) geography or (ii) asset class; and (b) whether there are thresholds that trigger warnings of excessive portfolio risks to the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (a) whether there are guidelines or restrictions on Statutory Boards and entities listed in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore with regard to investing in cryptocurrency-related assets; (b) if so, what are those guidelines or restrictions; and (c) whether all Statutory Boards and scheduled entities have fully adhered to those guidelines.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We encourage and support innovation in digital assets because we see potential for new technologies to transform cross-border payments, trade and settlement, as well as capital market activities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Early forecasts have proven too optimistic and it is still not clear that blockchain technology will develop beyond limited use cases into a gamechanger for a wide range of industries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is why we are piloting specific use cases to test the possibilities in the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are purely speculative as an investment asset and have no intrinsic value.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why MAS has consistently warned the retail public not to deal with them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Members have raised two broad issues in their questions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, on regulatory measures and the impact of the FTX bankruptcy on our financial system; and second, on the investments made by Temasek in FTX itself.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The collapse of FTX and other major cryptocurrency platforms should bring about much-needed rationalisation in the cryptocurrency space.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The repercussions on the cryptocurrency ecosystem globally are still unfolding and we are watching this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do not have data on the number of Singapore retail users of FTX, just as for other platforms that are not licensed here and do not operate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Unfortunately, those who invested in cryptocurrencies through FTX’s global platform would have lost money.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS’ surveillance shows that key financial institutions in Singapore have insignificant exposures to cryptocurrency and crypto players.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS has explained its approach to regulating financial institutions providing cryptocurrency services, also known as digital payment token (DPT) service providers, in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Such DPT service providers are regulated by MAS to address money laundering, terrorist financing and technology risks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Whether the DPT service providers can address these risks robustly is a key consideration in licensing them to operate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Importantly, DPT service providers are, currently, not regulated for safety and soundness, nor for investor protection.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is also the prevailing approach in most jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS has been consistently warning since 2017 that dealing in cryptocurrencies is hazardous.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS has also in its recent statements explained the role of MAS’ Investor Alert List (IAL) and why FTX was not listed on it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The IAL serves a very specific purpose: to warn the public of entities that may be wrongly perceived as being regulated by MAS, especially those which solicit Singapore customers without the requisite licence.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS did not have reason to list FTX on IAL because there was no evidence that it was soliciting users in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is unlike Binance, which was placed on IAL for actively soliciting users in Singapore without a valid licence and is being investigated presently by the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD) for possible violation of the Payment Services Act.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This does not mean that all entities which are not listed on IAL are safe to deal with.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MAS cannot possibly provide an exhaustive list of all the unsafe or unlicensed entities that exist in the world.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: After receiving industry and public feedback, MAS will finalise the proposals and implement appropriate regulatory measures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Cryptocurrency platforms can collapse due to fraud, unsustainable business models or excessive risk-taking.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: FTX is not the first cryptocurrency platform to collapse, nor will it be the last.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Further, even if a cryptocurrency platform is well-managed, cryptocurrencies themselves, as I mentioned earlier, are highly volatile and have no intrinsic value.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those who trade in cryptocurrencies must be prepared to lose all their value.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: No amount of regulation can remove this risk.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me address the Temasek investment in FTX and the Government's stance on our investment entities and Statutory Boards' exposure to digital assets and cryptocurrencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government does not prescribe guidelines on the allocation of specific assets or asset classes, whether for cryptocurrencies or other assets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This applies to our Statutory Boards, as well as our three investment entities managing our whole-of-Government assets, namely, Temasek, GIC and MAS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are not investment entities, but they have the flexibility to invest their surpluses and they, typically, do this through external fund managers, under the oversight of their respective supervising boards and Ministries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We expect Statutory Boards to make prudent investment decisions and not be distracted from their core functions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For our investment entities, the Government sets out its risk tolerance limits, monitors for appropriate diversification in asset classes, sectors and geographies and ensures that downside risks are not excessive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this spirit, the Government does not prescribe an exclusion list for specific assets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we expect the entities to incorporate environmental, social and governance, or ESG, considerations into their investment processes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They should do so in a way that best suits their investment mandates and preserves their reputation with global partners and markets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ultimately, the Government holds the boards and management teams responsible for formulating investment strategies in accordance with the Government's overall risk tolerance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: One of the areas Temasek and GIC's private equity arms operate in is new technology and early-stage companies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There will always be new waves of innovation and technology that seek to disrupt the status quo.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some waves will turn out to be hype and fizzle out over time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Other technologies will prove revolutionary and transformational, like the Internet.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But even with genuinely revolutionary technology, there are risks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many startups will fail, while a few will prove successful and grow into industry leaders, like Tencent or BioNTech.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The skill of venture capitalists lies in discerning the promising projects and backing them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Risk-taking is an essential part of such investments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As long-term investors, our investment entities have to operate in this space.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They do their best due diligence based on the information available.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Having made the investments, they monitor the investee companies closely, but no amount of due diligence and monitoring can eliminate the risks altogether.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is disappointing when there is a loss by our investment entities, as in the case of Temasek's investment in FTX.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even more so, because the loss arose from what turned out to be a very badly managed company and from possible fraud and mishandling of customer funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The fact that other leading global institutional investors, like BlackRock and Sequoia Capital, also invested in FTX does not mitigate this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What happened with FTX, therefore, has not only caused a financial loss to Temasek, but also reputational damage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Temasek recognises this and has issued a comprehensive statement to explain its due diligence process and the circumstances leading to its investment in FTX.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Temasek has also initiated an internal review by an independent team to study and improve its processes and to draw lessons for the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am confident that the Temasek board and management team will learn and improve from this experience.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, we should see this FTX loss in the broader context of Temasek's performance in early-stage investments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Following the FTX collapse, some Members have suggested implementing more guidelines and safeguards over the investments made by Temasek and GIC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is understandable, but the governance structures in place today for Temasek and GIC are already more extensive than those of a typical company.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Temasek, which is an investment holding company, is audited by commercial auditors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: GIC, which manages public funds, is audited by the Auditor-General.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Fifth Schedule entities, both Temasek and GIC are subject to the President's oversight of their budgets and key appointments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead, we should insulate the boards from political pressures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let them do their work, carry out their responsibilities and fulfil their investment mandates, commercially and professionally.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The investment entities themselves publish their performance with respect to broad market indices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In Temasek's case, the MSCI equities indices and, in GIC's case, the Reference Portfolio, comprising 65% global equities and 35% global bonds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These market indices and data from reputable global investment funds serve as useful references.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, ultimately, the Government evaluates the entities based on their long-term performance and their track records show that they have performed creditably, even in challenging environments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the occurrence of investment losses does not, in itself, imply that the governance system is not working.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Rather, this is the nature of investment and risk-taking.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What is important is that our investment entities take lessons from each failure and success and continue to take well-judged risks in order to achieve good overall returns in the long term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this way, we can continue to add to our national reserves and provide a stable income stream to fund Government programmes for a long time to come.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One, may I ask if FTX is the only cryptocurrency-related investment that the three investment entities are exposed to?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Two, despite the failings of cryptocurrencies, the blockchain-based digital infrastructure may still prove to be useful in other aspects.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, may I ask, for these investment entities, whether they have been or will continue to invest in such companies and, if they have been, how has the investment performance been so far?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These investments are within the overall context of the risk parameters set out by the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, in GIC's case, it has a broadly diversified global portfolio.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, if we talk about concerns of a broader fallout, I think that it would be relatively contained.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, as the Member has highlighted, there may be promising use cases in blockchains.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But as I have mentioned in my reply, some of the earlier optimism about blockchains has proven to be too optimistic.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Remember, a few months ago, there was a lot of enthusiasm.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even within this House, Members were suggesting for MAS to move faster.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And MAS was being criticised for being too slow.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that general enthusiasm has proven to be overly optimistic.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Will there be specific use cases where blockchain technologies can be applied and be promising?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Well, we are pursuing pilots in MAS, specifically in the financial sector.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And the investment entities themselves, therefore, will have to do their own due diligence in analysing each particular case that comes up and consider whether or not to invest in these projects.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think that given global banks' exposure to digital assets and some exposure to cryptocurrencies, does an investment entity like MAS, for example, do they build in the risk to cryptocurrencies and digital assets blowing up as part of their worst-case scenarios in their stress test scenarios?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, for financial institutions and non-bank financial institutions, especially on cryptocurrencies' downside risks worst-case scenarios.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is quite important, given that the systemically important institutions may have ramifications on Singaporeans in general.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we still apply these stress tests, not just to Singapore's institutions, but to the broader global operating environment to determine how this will impact Singapore's financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is part of our continued risk monitoring, not only for MAS and the financial sector, but also for the Government's overall investment portfolio.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And under current statutes and regulations, are Temasek, GIC and MAS free to invest in anything they want to, as long as their own boards or management teams approve them and they fall within the risk tolerance level?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The keys to any successful long-term reserve management systems are governance, professional management and a long-term horizon.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And the President is part of this governance process, too, because she, in terms of the appointments of people, has the powers as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, within that governance system that we have in place, there are processes, there are risk metrics to monitor, there are clear accountabilities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And it is a system that has worked well over the decades and has delivered good long-term outcomes for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Just a few questions for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But he also said that the Government monitors the portfolios, if I heard him correctly, for geographic diversification and downside risks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am just a little curious how those two things are reconciled.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What kind of discussion will the Government have, if it monitors those risks and diversification and feels that they are off?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does the Government actually intervene and would that not then be prescriptive if such a situation arose?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I was just hoping the Deputy Prime Minister could expand on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My second supplementary question is on the rotational audits by the Auditor-General's Office (AGO).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would just like to ask why that is the case, since they are both managing public funds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It could be argued that Temasek has the legal form of a private company but, against that, I would say that right now, AGO does audit Ministries and Statutory Boards that own private companies, for example, MOH Holdings or EDB Investments, and presumably those companies under a Statutory Board are also subject to rotational audits by AGO.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, the fact that Temasek is a private entity should not, in and of itself, mean that it does not need to be subject to rotational audits by AGO.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My last supplementary question is really, would the —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Please keep it to two supplementary questions for now, please.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, the risk tolerance, the amount of risk that the Government has set out for GIC is expressed in our reference portfolio 65/35.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That sets out the kinds of risks that the Government is prepared for GIC to take and, therefore, GIC, as an active manager, publishes its performance with regard to that risk and the performance that it tracks with regard to the referenced portfolio.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in its annual Temasek Review, Temasek will put out some of its risk considerations and its risk parameters.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, to the extent that these risks are disclosed, the investment entities do have disclosures through their respective platforms – largely through their annual reports.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We monitor the portfolios, we get data, we get information, we monitor them, we subject these portfolios to stress tests, given something that collapses in an extraneous event that takes place, a crisis, a fallout in cryptocurrencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We subject them to rigorous stress tests to make sure that the overall portfolio, even under these stress tests, does not have significant losses beyond the threshold that we think would be too much.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if, indeed, the stress tests show that there is too much risk being taken or concentration of a particular asset that may lead to some vulnerabilities, then we provide feedback to the entities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They have the discretion then to take the necessary actions, to adjust.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is how we operate; not by prescribing but monitoring and setting in place overall risk parameters from which our entities operate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On audit, it is not unusual at all for private auditors to audit even public agencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Statutory Boards themselves are subject to commercial auditors, private auditors, not to the Auditor-General.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, unless we are suggesting that somehow these private auditors are not as good as the Auditor-General, I do not see any reason why.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not unusual that the Auditor-General has a remit, largely within the Public Service and Government Ministries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But for some Statutory Boards, for a commercial entity like Temasek, which also, within it, has a portfolio of listed entities, well, I think we should let commercial auditors do their job.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And so far, they have been doing a very good job.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There really is not any obligation to put funds into trust accounts in banks for safeguarding because digital assets are mainly on chain and not in the vault.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I note that the Deputy Prime Minister mentioned that there is now a consultation on reviews of regulatory approaches.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could help to reduce the risk of misuse of digital assets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Part of the proposal covers some of the things that the Member has talked about.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will finalise these proposals after the consultation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There may be more feedback, including suggestions from Members, which MAS will study.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, as I said in my reply, no amount of regulation can eliminate all the risks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It can go all the way to zero and people who want to trade in that must be prepared to lose all their money.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, because the reserves are the money of the people, accountability is important.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And especially in a case like FTX, there are many unanswered questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I have two questions for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, the Deputy Prime Minister has answered that the investment guidelines are available in separate places, like in the report of Temasek and in some places for GIC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are things that Singaporeans would like to know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, will the Government in the future prepare all these guidelines in a consolidated place so that Singaporeans know the investment strategy and the guidelines guiding the investment of our sovereign funds?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, then whether that report will be made available in a future session in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I will answer all three questions and indulge Mr Leong Mun Wai.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the first question whether we might consolidate all the information, well, they are just three entities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Actually, more like two, because MAS is quite unique.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Its investments are really in very conservative instruments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, really, there are just all of two entities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you think about it, go to the GIC website, go to the Temasek website.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If Members think it is useful, MOF can put up links on our website to both websites, so that you can refer to them at your own pleasure and your own time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is very unusual, first of all, for Temasek or GIC for that matter, to comment on individual investments – they do not, as a normal practice.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because we should not get into the habit of looking at individual investments in retrospect.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There will always be ups and downs, and there will always be successes and failures in investments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All of that is on the Temasek website, including a series of FAQs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, all of that is available on the Temasek website.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The third question, I have answered that, too.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister in his reply talked about the over-optimism in the earlier stages of the crypto developments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We also know that many financial centres like Dubai and Hong Kong are all aspiring to be the cryptocurrency hub.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister whether the Government sees hubbing the cryptocurrency trading activities in Singapore as necessary to strengthen our position as a financial centre.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What are the possible economic use cases here?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have always looked at how we can be a responsible and innovative digital asset player and the focus is on "responsible" and "innovative".

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where innovation is concerned, as I mentioned just now, some of the earlier optimism about blockchain technologies has been proven to be not well-placed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think there is now a more realistic sense of what these technologies can do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are now continuing with pilot projects on payments, on capital markets, on settlements, to work out what are the promising use cases for such technologies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And within that context, there may be a role for DPT service providers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if these DPT service providers do exist in Singapore, are licensed here – and DPT service providers would include exchanges for cryptocurrencies and tokens – then they will be licensed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: After our consultations, we will want to put in place these tightened measures for the licensed entities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just have one supplementary question for the Deputy Prime Minister on his reply to my earlier supplementary question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, it is just one, you can count me on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Of course, Ministries, Statutory Boards are subject to commercial external auditors and that includes the private companies under them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And GIC is also subject to commercial external auditors, as is Temasek.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But Ministries, Statutory Boards, GIC and the private companies under Ministries and Statutory Boards are also subject, on top of that, to the Auditor-General's audits.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not believe they have been answered in the Minister's answer earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, which funds are these and how do they compare?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The published references are the GIC Reference Portfolio as well as the MSCI equities indices, which are published by both GIC and Temasek respectively.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you look at both entities' performance vis-à-vis these reference points, they have done well, in fact.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They have done well over the long term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We also track the performance of other fund managers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in fact, many of these fund managers' performances are published.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Anyone can look at how private equities have done – top quintile, top quantile – asset managers, how they have done over the long term.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, anyone can look at that data and compare that with GIC and Temasek's performance, which is also published.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On losses, whether or not we require specific audits or reviews to be done, losses happen all the time as part of the investment process.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, you have to really take that into consideration and look at the overall portfolio rather than look at each individual project that does not do well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in this case, because it is such an exceptional situation, it has gotten so much publicity, it has also impacted Temasek reputationally, Temasek itself has undertaken its review, it has put out information and it has taken the extra step of doing a further review; which it has also said it will do – an internal review, led by an independent team reporting to the board, with the purpose of looking at how it can learn from this experience and improve its own processes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the Minister shared that licensed DPT service providers are required to put in place a risk assessment test, among other things.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, as such measures have yet to be put in place, unlicensed service providers, such as FTX, could still have conducted business activities in Singapore with our retail customers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How does the Government intend to address this gap?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, given the concerns around the viability of blockchain and crypto-related industries, will the Minister be willing to share what is the number of companies' dollar value and percentage exposure to service providers and technology infrastructure players related to blockchain and the digital asset space to assure Singaporeans, especially when The Straits Times reported on 24 November that GIC is an investor in the group, with ties to troubled cryptocurrency broker Genesis Trading?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even if we have a very comprehensive system in Singapore, it does not stop Singaporeans from going overseas or going online to overseas platforms to invest in cryptocurrency.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is not going to stop that from happening.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think what we should do is focus on what are reasonable regulations, learning from the recent experiences and put in place a sound regulatory system but, at the same time, continue with the reminders and public education we have been doing all this while for so many years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will step up our efforts there to let people know the risk of investing in cryptocurrency, that this is highly volatile, it has no intrinsic value; and, really, anyone who does this has to go in with their eyes open.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the second question, I have already actually answered that in the context of Ms Tin Pei Ling's first supplementary question, setting out the investments that our investment entities make in this digital asset space within the context of their holdings in early-stage companies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But that is the whole point of diversification in investments.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do appreciate and understand that losses are part and parcel of the investment landscape.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I do not think anyone questions when Temasek makes money.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But there are two fallouts to this particular collapse of FTX.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are scammers, opportunists taking advantage of the situation, setting up websites for people to come forward to make claims.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would MAS be looking into how to protect our Singaporean retail investors in this regard?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would Temasek be looking to reserve its rights to make any particular claim, should the need arise?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am sure Temasek is on top of this and will reserve its rights to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Whether it is in the crypto space, whether it is SMS – there is a whole range of different scams.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we have set up a task force specifically on scams and we will do whatever we can to address this problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just following up on the Deputy Prime Minister's replies to some of the supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With regard to Temasek's independent review of the FTX imbroglio, this independent review, is it an external one, external to Temasek, or is it internal, a Temasek team reporting on Temasek's investment in FTX?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, they will be separate, they will not be clouded by what steps were taken and they will report directly to the board, as I mentioned just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What further actions might MOF, as shareholder or Government, take?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Is this sufficient in this case or what thresholds will be reached in order for us to trigger further action?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Quite aside from this case, for which Temasek is doing its part and is pursuing this review, which I would add, separately, that it does this for FTX, but it actually also has done this in the past before when there are similar instances.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But when there are instances where, for example, there is a write-off in an investment project, where there is a permanent impairment and it is an investment that did not go well, then they would initiate something like this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They have done this before and that is what they are doing again.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a step-up from their usual review process, which applies to all investments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this case, as has happened in the past, Temasek feels that this is a significant project and there is something to be learnt from the experience, so, they are undertaking this separate review.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Will we go beyond such a separate review to call in external auditors, for example?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will not rule out if something like that were to happen.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, in these situations, the mood among investors and investment-related decision-makers can change as the narrative shifts.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask whether the Deputy Prime Minister foresees the possibility that investors and investment entities will shy away and have a chilling effect on their appetite for high potential, long-term investments that, nevertheless, have good fundamentals?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because in the Science and Technology sector, there have been investments and developments with a long horizon that bore fruit many years later – whether it was the vaccines that allowed us to fight COVID-19, whether it is monoclonal antibodies that took years to become viable treatments for diseases and so on.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is precisely the advantage that we have as investors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a very important strategic advantage that GIC and Temasek have.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To have that long-term perspective and not just to focus on the short-term or follow and chase after fads; and then, if the market cycle comes down, you quickly sell your assets and cut your losses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our investment entities do recognise this and there is an appropriate allocation in their portfolios for such investments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And they will continue to take such risks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I hope everyone in this House recognises this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why it is important we insulate our investment entities from these political pressures and let them do their jobs well, commercially and professionally, as they have been doing all these years.
